assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opened a new observational window: detecting high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with a cubic-kilometre Antarctic detector is a landmark of instrument building. The diffuse flux, the TXS 0506+056 association and the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results show neutrinos can probe cosmic-ray accelerators that light cannot. This is the kind of detector-driven discovery that lasts.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the IceCube project and its science case; Karle led detector construction and the optical-module and ice-calibration work. Yoshida is credited with important contributions, but the decisive pair for a compact prize looks like Halzen and Karle. Collaboration-scale credit means any allocation omits many contributors, and the committee would need expert advice on the historical roles (AMANDA, IceCube).
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux was seen in 2013 and has been confirmed with several independent channels and analyses. Source identification is at a few sigma and still maturing. Timing is good because the observational window is established and the instrument is well calibrated, although the source physics is still evolving.
uncertainties: I rely on memory for the individual roles within the IceCube collaboration and have not verified them.
Source association is at about 3 to 4 sigma for individual objects, and independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD is not yet at comparable sensitivity.
Whether the Nobel record already treats neutrino detection as recognised (2002) may affect how the committee frames novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, based on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is a decisive gain in measurement precision with consequences for time standards, tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and searches for dark matter. It is a clean instrument-driven advance.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice-clock concept and first demonstrated it; Ye led the group that took the strontium clock to record accuracy and coherence. The two-name configuration is compact and clean with little dispute that I know of. Others, such as Takamoto, Lemke and Ludlow, are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Several independent labs across continents have reproduced and improved the clocks over roughly twenty years, and redefinition of the second is under discussion. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: The 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for ion trapping could be seen as partially overlapping, which is a framing issue.
I am an astroparticle experimentalist, so I would rely on AMO colleagues to assess priority between Katori and Ye's group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BeppoSAX X-ray afterglow of GRB 970228 and the optical redshift measurements established that gamma-ray bursts are cosmological, resolving a long-standing puzzle. It is a clear, consequential observational discovery that led to a whole field, though it is astrophysics more than fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Costa led the BeppoSAX Wide Field Camera localisation and Frontera the gamma-ray burst monitor; Kulkarni's group delivered the optical, radio and redshift follow-up that fixed the distance scale. The supplied credit supports a three-person prize, but Jan van Paradijs, who made the first optical counterpart and died in 1999, cannot be recognised, and Paczynski, Piro and others are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Afterglows have been observed for more than 25 years with many missions, and the cosmological origin is firmly established, together with later links to supernovae and kilonovae. It is arguably late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the prize rewards a discovery of astrophysical nature fits the physics criterion in the committee's view is a judgement call.
The credit split between the X-ray localisation and the optical identification is genuinely contestable, and the loss of a key contributor complicates it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a designed, band-structure-engineered semiconductor light source, built from intersubband transitions in a superlattice, giving mid-infrared and terahertz emission. It is original, a device invention with lasting impact in gas sensing and spectroscopy, and a very good fit for the instrument-building tradition.
assessment.attribution: Capasso led the Bell Labs team that proposed and demonstrated the QCL in 1994, and Faist was the lead author of the first demonstration and later drove room-temperature and continuous-wave operation. Cho supplied the molecular-beam-epitaxy growth that made the structures possible, which is important but I would treat it as enabling craft. Three names are possible, and two is the cleaner prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Three decades of independent development, commercial deployment and many extensions to terahertz and frequency combs show stable impact.
uncertainties: Whether a laser device invention counts as a physics discovery in the way committee precedent has treated lasers like blue LEDs and chirped pulse amplification needs discussion.
The weight to give Cho's growth contribution compared with the design concept is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED created strong coupling between a single photon and a superconducting qubit on a chip. It is the basis for superconducting quantum processors and a natural successor to the 2025 recognition of macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. The impact on quantum technology is very large.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal; Wallraff and Schoelkopf's group performed the 2004 experiment. A three-person configuration of Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin is plausible but leaves Blais out; the credit between theory and experiment is not clear to me. This is outside my own field and I would rely on colleagues for the details.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced in many groups, but the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis might make a close follow-up premature or seem repetitive within the committee.
uncertainties: The overlap with the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits is a framing and timing risk.
The best three-person configuration is disputed, because four names are credited and Devoret's own circuit work, which is not in the list, is also part of the story.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened the field of twistronics. A prediction of flat bands at a specific twist angle was followed by the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and by a very large wave of follow-on work on moire materials. The originality and rate of impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 flat-band prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group (with Cao as lead experimentalist) made the 2018 observations. The credit set is plausible for a theory-experiment prize, but Yuan Cao is not in the supplied names, which could be a fairness concern.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent reproduction of the correlated insulators and superconductivity exists across many labs, although the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated. It might be a little early for a prize of this kind.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is still unsettled, so the interpretation is not yet stable.
The omission of the first author of the 2018 experiments is a potential attribution problem.
I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the weight of the theory prediction relative to the experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays offer a way to detect the nanohertz gravitational-wave background using the exquisitely stable millisecond pulsars as a galactic-scale detector. It is a beautiful use of a natural instrument, and it complements LIGO's high-frequency band.
assessment.attribution: The supplied names reflect leadership of the EPTA/PPTA/NANOGrav efforts, but the result rests on several competing collaborations with hundreds of members and very long observing baselines, so a clean three-person allocation is hard. Hellings and Downs, Detweiler and others made the foundational contributions to the method.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 evidence is at roughly 3 to 4 sigma for the Hellings-Downs correlation and its origin (supermassive black-hole binaries versus new physics) is open, so I consider recognition premature until the detection is confirmed at higher significance.
uncertainties: Detection significance is below the usual five-sigma standard and has not been independently combined and confirmed at that level.
The astrophysical source of the signal is not established.
Collaboration structure complicates a fair choice of up to three laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave interference into a precision instrument for gravimetry, measurement of the gravitational constant and the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. It is a measurement technique with a wide range of applications, which fits my instrument-oriented view.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard made early atom-interferometer demonstrations, Bordé developed the theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer foundations, and Kasevich developed the precision light-pulse devices. Steven Chu and others are not in the supplied credit, and the 1997 and 2001 prizes already covered related cooling and condensate work, so the attribution is awkward.
assessment.maturity: Technology is mature and independently implemented, but the scientific headline results (such as equivalence-principle tests at the 1e-12 level) are not as dramatic as other candidates, and it is not clear a single decisive discovery is being recognised.
uncertainties: The credit for the foundational idea is spread over several groups and there is no obvious canonical trio.
Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes may reduce novelty for the committee.
I am not an AMO specialist and would defer to colleagues on priority.
